text: {"thinking":"The manufacturer records establish that 2,000 GPUs were delivered to Eemshaven. Compare the operator’s system list with those serial ranges to identify any inventory gaps and map the clusters and feeds for independent checks.","action":"system_list","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The manufacturer confirms delivery of 2,000 GPUs in two serial blocks. Compare the site list with both blocks to identify which GPUs, power feeds, and links the audit can cover.","action":"system_list","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The listed clusters account for all 2,000 GPUs in the manufacturer’s shipment records by count. Check the grid operator’s full 30-day record for sustained load or unexplained energy that can guide targeted sensor checks.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The listed clusters account for all 2,000 GPUs in the manufacturer’s shipment records, although the site list gives no serial numbers to verify individual assignments. Check the grid operator’s records for sustained load, daily demand patterns, and unexplained consumption across the full audit window.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The grid records show brief load increases on F1 on days 3–5 and 14–15 and on F2 on days 10–11. Power alone cannot distinguish short training runs from batch inference or reveal training hidden in the steady load. Use the sealed logs to identify recorded job sizes, timing, and labels for comparison with independent measurements.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Grid records show elevated load on F1 during days 5–11 and on F2 during days 17–19. Compare both periods with the internet provider's full-month outbound records for evidence of interactive demand. Low outbound traffic would leave both training and batch inference plausible.","action":"outbound_traffic","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Grid records show sustained extra load on F1 on days 12–19 and a shorter increase on F2 on days 10–11. Sample Cluster A on day 15, in the middle of the F1 plateau. The independent tap can help distinguish training from batch inference, both of which can sustain high power.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":15}}

{"thinking":"A run may be split across labels or clusters, so check recorded timing against independent interconnect measurements. Separate customers may have run legitimate jobs, so check registration, payments, and whether their clusters exchanged data. Batch inference or cooling may explain the load, so compare spectra and interconnect traffic with live chip probes. An unlisted cluster could host training, so reconcile the manufacturer’s inventory with metered feeds. Missing records or late payments may explain discrepancies, so check escrow timestamps and bank records. Inventory matches by count, and every escrow copy matches the current log. Read the job entries to identify when and where to test these explanations.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Outbound traffic stayed steady during both load spikes, leaving batch inference and training plausible. Sample Cluster A on day 6, during its peak load, to distinguish inference-level traffic from ordinary or low-traffic training and focus the GPU-hour investigation.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":6}}

{"thinking":"The escrow recovers the missing days and shows that a fine-tune on B was recorded when the logs were sealed. Check whether the listed workloads account for the metered energy and whether the three load increases or the steady baseline warrant independent workload checks.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s listed links carried traffic consistent with inference on day 15, far below even the low-communication training benchmark. The F1 power plateau still warrants an independent check because the tap covers only listed links. Check F1 for a training-like periodic signal on the same day so the two measurements can be compared.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":15}}

{"thinking":"The balance checks leave a log gap and an unpaid invoice. The escrow confirms that the B fine-tune was recorded at the time. Get the full job timeline to identify customer and node allocations, then use independent traffic measurements to test whether the load peaks or steady baseline reflect one coordinated run.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s day 6 traffic is consistent with ordinary training and far above the expected inference rate. The tap covers the whole cluster, so it cannot tell whether one run or several produced that traffic. Check the sealed scheduler records for job boundaries, GPU allocations, and customer labels across both load spikes, then test those records against independent measurements.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The escrow confirms the logs match what Borealis submitted each day. Read the scheduler entries to identify the jobs declared during both power increases, then check their GPU counts, dates, and customer identities against independent evidence.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The escrow confirms that the presented logs match the copies submitted each night. The scheduler details can show whether the two load spikes were recorded as single jobs, concurrent jobs, or successive phases. Use those allocations for the fixed balance checks, then test the recorded run boundaries against independent evidence.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The two consecutive Cluster A fine-tuning jobs total 50,400 GPU-hours if they were phases of one run. The day 6 tap supports training activity, and the escrow establishes that the labels were recorded at the time. Neither establishes whether the jobs were independent. Run the fixed balance checks to compare the recorded allocations with the independent measurements and identify discrepancies to investigate.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The sealed logs place a 7,200 GPU-hour fine-tune on B and a 134,400 GPU-hour job labelled batch on A. A’s listed links carried inference-level traffic on day 15, and the periodic power signal could come from either workload. Check independent bank records for both customers before asking them to confirm what they ran. A missing payment could reflect ordinary billing delays.","action":"bank_payments","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s day 20 traffic is consistent with inference. Check cluster B on the same day to see whether its steady load also fits inference or indicates undeclared training.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"B","day":20}}

{"thinking":"The balance checks show that the declared records fit the totals. Test whether F1’s steady load includes unrecorded training by sampling Cluster A on day 27, when no scheduled job is logged. Traffic above inference levels would justify checking other dates for duration and using a live chip probe to corroborate the workload.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":27}}

{"thinking":"Meridian paid its invoice, which confirms payment but leaves the workload and customer independence unresolved. Check Meridian’s ownership in the company register and ask what it ran on Cluster A during days 12–19.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Meridian Analytics"}}

{"thinking":"Both clusters showed inference-like traffic on day 20. The largest load spike was on cluster A on day 14, when the scheduler recorded a batch job. Sample that day to check whether GPU-to-GPU traffic fits batch inference or suggests training under the batch label.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":14}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s day 27 traffic is consistent with inference and far below even the low-communication training benchmark. Cluster B also had steady power and no logged job that day. Sample its internal links to test whether that load included unrecorded training.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"B","day":27}}

{"thinking":"Both clusters had inference-level internal traffic on day 27. A training run could have ended before then. Sample Cluster A on day 12, when F1 was at its usual load and the scheduler listed no job there, to test whether that baseline concealed training earlier in the month.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":12}}

{"thinking":"Ostara’s registration supports its existence, and its silence leaves the job boundary unresolved. Measure F1 on the last day of the Tidewater allocation to establish a power signature for comparison with the first day of the Ostara allocation. Allow for normal frequency drift when comparing the two days.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":7}}

{"thinking":"F1 showed a steady 0.42 Hz line on day 7. Check F1 on day 8, when the scheduler records the handoff. A clear change in the power signature would support separate workloads, while a similar line would be consistent with continuity. Either result needs corroboration because frequencies can drift and separate jobs can have similar signatures.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":8}}

{"thinking":"The outbound shortfall early in the job and the surge on day 19 fit a batch job that held its results for a final export. Site-wide traffic cannot tie that export to Meridian. Sample Cluster A on day 13 to check whether the listed links also carried inference-level traffic early in the power plateau. Training-level traffic would challenge the batch explanation, while another low reading would still leave unlisted links outside coverage.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":13}}

{"thinking":"F1 shifted from 0.42 Hz on day 7 to 0.58 Hz on day 8, the recorded handoff. That supports separate runs, though a single run changing GPU allocation or workload could also shift frequency. Check day 9 to see whether the new signature persists during the Ostara allocation.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":9}}

{"thinking":"F1 showed no periodic line on day 20. The earlier taps sampled only links within each cluster, so they did not test whether a run spanned both clusters. Sample the A–B links on day 20, when both feeds were at baseline and no job was logged, to distinguish ordinary inference traffic from sustained cross-cluster GPU communication.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":20}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s listed links carried inference-level traffic on two days of the power plateau, and the final-day outbound surge fits a bulk export. The separate F2 power increase on days 10–11 still needs an independent workload check. Sample Cluster B during that increase to see whether its traffic is consistent with the declared fine-tune or points to more training activity than recorded.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"B","day":11}}

{"thinking":"Lumen Health’s unpaid invoice could be an ordinary payment delay or a cover for undeclared training. Check the company register and ask Lumen directly what workload it ran and when.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Lumen Health"}}

{"thinking":"The power signature changed at the recorded handoff and stayed near the new frequency on day 9. That supports separate workloads, but a single run could have changed its configuration. Check who actually paid for each job and whether the bank records tie each payment to its invoice. The billing check established payment, while Ostara’s role remains unconfirmed.","action":"bank_payments","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s day 7 tap found inference-level traffic. Cluster B has only been sampled on day 27, leaving its steady load earlier in the month largely unchecked. Sample B on day 14, when its power was at baseline and no job was logged there. Inference-level traffic would support the ordinary-load explanation for B that day. Elevated traffic would warrant checking whether it persisted or coincided with traffic between A and B.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"B","day":14}}

{"thinking":"Day 20 traffic within and between the clusters fits inference. A run active on other days could still exceed 50,000 GPU-hours. Check F1 on day 27, when the grid shows baseline load and the scheduler lists no training. A periodic line would warrant a live follow-up and could also come from batch inference or cooling.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":27}}

{"thinking":"Grid records show sustained extra load on F1 during days 20–28 and a shorter rise on F2 during days 10–11. Retrieve the sealed scheduler records to see how each episode was recorded at the time. Then use independent measurements to test whether the loads came from batch inference, separate training jobs, or one coordinated run.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Day 20 traffic and day 27 power readings support the inference explanation for the sampled dates. The earlier baseline remains untested. Check F1 on day 8, between the first two recorded fine-tunes, for a periodic signal that could indicate undeclared training. A line would also be consistent with some inference or cooling activity and would need corroboration.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":8}}

{"thinking":"The short F2 rise could be Ostara Legal’s recorded fine-tune. Check it against grid energy, customer records, and sampled GPU traffic. The sustained F1 rise could be genuine batch inference, several independent training jobs, or one coordinated run recorded as batch. Compare GPU traffic and power signatures, and use a live chip probe if the job is still active. A scheduling or accounting error could also explain a mismatch. Cross-check the records against the grid and any relevant bank or customer evidence. Run the fixed balance checks first to identify which discrepancies need follow-up.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The day 8 power reading found no periodic line on cluster A. Sample cluster B’s listed links on that same early baseline day to see whether its traffic fits inference or indicates undeclared training, including training designed to exchange less data.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"B","day":8}}

{"thinking":"The outbound shortfall overlaps the 700-GPU job on A. Internal batch inference could send little traffic to the internet, and training could produce the same shortfall. Sample A’s GPU-to-GPU traffic on day 24, when the job was active, to distinguish inference from ordinary or low-traffic training. The sample alone cannot establish how many GPUs belonged to one run or how long it lasted.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":24}}

{"thinking":"The day-24 tap strongly favors training on A over ordinary batch inference. It measures aggregate traffic and cannot distinguish one coordinated run from several concurrent runs. Probe GPUs across A’s scheduled pool while the load is still active, with an interactive GPU on A and a GPU on B for comparison. The probe can corroborate training on the chips presented. Run identity and duration still need independent evidence.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0501","A-0600","A-0700","A-0800","A-0900","A-1000","A-1100","A-1200","A-0250","B-0450"],"hour":640}}

{"thinking":"Grid records show a sustained rise on both GPU feeds on days 5–16 and a smaller rise on F1 on days 19–20. Check the sealed scheduler records for job timing, GPU allocations, and customer labels across both intervals. Use those records to target independent checks of workload type and coordination.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"F1 had one steady line near 0.88 Hz on day 24, when the optical tap showed heavy GPU-to-GPU traffic. Check day 20, the first day of elevated F1 load. A similar line would support a persistent workload across the two days. A different pattern would prompt a check for job turnover or concurrent runs. The spectrum alone cannot establish run identity or GPU count.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":20}}

{"thinking":"The company register links Quillon Tech to Borealis, and Quillon’s reply confirms only the invoice. Check a declared customer on cluster A for independent ownership and an account of its training job. This will help test whether the substantial traffic between A and B is consistent with the claimed separation of the jobs.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Corvid Labs"}}

{"thinking":"The manufacturer records 2,600 GPU deliveries. Compare the operator’s system list with those records to identify which GPUs and feeds are accounted for. Any gap could reflect spares, transfers, or unlisted capacity. Test those explanations against grid energy and independent sensor readings.","action":"system_list","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Escrow confirms the days 5–16 load was absent from the logs as filed. An independent tap on the A–B link can test whether the two clusters exchanged traffic consistent with a coordinated run or operated independently. Day 12 falls in the middle of the sustained load.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":12}}

{"thinking":"The operator lists 2,000 GPUs against 2,600 delivered. The 600-unit gap could reflect spares, transfers, or unlisted compute. Check the grid operator’s energy records across days 1–30 for sustained load on F3 or elsewhere that could distinguish active hardware from unused inventory. Energy alone cannot identify a training run.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The independent tap measured 181 GB/s of GPU-to-GPU traffic between A and B on day 12, during the twelve-day rise on both feeds. That makes ordinary batch inference and wholly independent cluster workloads less plausible. The sealed logs omit this interval. Run the fixed balance checks to quantify what the recorded jobs leave unexplained before testing whether the load came from one coordinated training run.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The day-20 tap places training-scale communication at the start of the F1 load increase. Check F1 on day 27, when five sampled GPUs read as training. A similar steady line would strengthen the case for continuity across the window. A changed pattern would give us a lead to check for job turnover or concurrent runs. The spectrum cannot establish run identity or GPU count on its own.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":27}}

{"thinking":"F3 carried a steady 0.91 Hz line on day 26, the last day of elevated load. Check day 2, when the elevated load began, for a line near the same frequency. A match would support a persistent source across the interval, with training, batch inference, and periodic cooling still in contention.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F3","day":2}}

{"thinking":"The balance checks flag unexplained energy on both GPU feeds throughout days 5–16. The day 12 cross-cluster traffic makes ordinary batch inference unlikely, but one day's traffic cannot establish how long a single training process ran. Check F1 on the same day for a training-like power signature that can be compared across feeds and dates.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":12}}

{"thinking":"The cross-cluster traffic persisted through day 28, but the tap cannot identify which jobs generated it. Check whether a third listed customer can independently substantiate a separate fine-tune.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Pallas Systems"}}

{"thinking":"F1 showed a steady 0.85 Hz line on day 12, when the optical tap measured 181 GB/s between the clusters. Check F2 on the same day. A matching line would strengthen the case for a shared workload, while the duration of that workload still needs checking.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F2","day":12}}

{"thinking":"F3’s elevated load and similar periodic lines at both ends of days 2–26 support a sustained workload. Training, batch inference, and periodic cooling remain plausible. Check whether independently measured outbound traffic rises and falls with F3’s load. A matching change would support inference serving external users. Flat traffic would leave local batch inference and cooling in contention.","action":"outbound_traffic","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The register links three billed customers to Borealis, and their replies confirm only the invoices. The optical tap shows that heavy A–B traffic appeared with the synchronized fine-tunes and persisted through day 28. To test whether one training process dominated both clusters or a smaller shared workload ran alongside separate jobs, look for a periodic signature on F1 on day 26, when the tap measured 228 GB/s, for comparison with F2 on the same day.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":26}}

{"thinking":"Both GPU feeds showed similar periodic lines on day 12, when the optical tap measured 181 GB/s between clusters. Sample the same link on day 5, the first day of the sustained load, to test whether heavy cross-cluster traffic was already present or was confined to a shorter episode.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":5}}

{"thinking":"The switch counter gives 0.3 GB/s without specifying what it averages, so it cannot be compared directly with the optical tap’s cluster-wide total. The first chip probe covered only A-0501 through A-0900 on day 27. Probe five previously untested nodes higher in the scheduled range on day 26. Training readings there would support a broader training footprint and weaken the explanation that the earlier readings came from a small workload alongside synthetic data generation. The probe cannot establish whether the chips share a run.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0925","A-1000","A-1075","A-1150","A-1200"],"hour":610}}

{"thinking":"The escrow confirms that all 30 daily submissions match the current logs. Run the fixed balance checks to see whether recorded jobs and listed equipment account for the sustained F3 load and the 600-GPU inventory gap. Use any discrepancy to guide follow-up on cooling, batch inference, or unlisted training.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Heavy cross-cluster traffic on days 5, 12, and 16 supports sustained coordination, but successive training runs could produce similar daily averages. Check F1 on day 5 for a full-day periodic signature comparable to the 0.85 Hz line on day 12.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":5}}

{"thinking":"A single coordinated run could explain the steady load and heavy cross-cluster traffic on days 5, 12, and 16. Successive shorter runs could also fit those measurements. Check whether F1's full-day line near 0.85 Hz persisted to day 16, when the tap still showed heavy traffic.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":16}}

{"thinking":"F1 shifted from 0.89 Hz on day 26 to 0.91 Hz on day 28. Check whether F2 shifted in the same direction while cross-cluster traffic remained high. A similar shift would favor a shared training process over separate fine-tunes with coincidentally similar step times, though it would leave the number of participating GPUs uncertain.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F2","day":28}}

{"thinking":"Nine of ten sampled GPUs across A’s scheduled pool read as training. The inference reading could reflect a mixed workload or probe error. The optical tap and probe favor training, but neither identifies run boundaries. Check the cooling feed on day 24 for a line near F1’s 0.88 Hz signal. A matching line would weaken the use of that signal as evidence of one persistent run. An absent line would leave coordination unresolved.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F0","day":24}}

{"thinking":"The cooling-feed measurement found no matching line on day 24. A’s traffic, chip readings, and recurring F1 line favor sustained training, but they leave run boundaries unresolved. Follow up on the separate F2 load rise by checking whether Ostara Legal independently confirms the timing and scale of the recorded 7,200 GPU-hour fine-tune.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Ostara Legal"}}

{"thinking":"The bank response covers customer invoices and leaves the claimed GPU resale unverified. Check the full scheduler log for node assignments, job dates, and customer labels that could connect the F3 load to recorded activity or identify where to direct an independent check. The escrow confirms when the records were submitted, while their contents still depend on the operator.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Ostara independently confirmed the 7,200 GPU-hour fine-tune that accounts for the F2 rise. On A, grid load, optical traffic and chip readings favor sustained training. Check F1 on day 22, midway between the first two spectrum readings. A break or additional line could point to turnover or overlapping runs. A steady line near the existing readings would support continuity, though it cannot identify which GPUs trained together.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":22}}

{"thinking":"The scheduler lists no job that explains F3’s elevated load on days 2–26. Check F3 near the middle of that interval for a line resembling the ones on days 2 and 26. A match would support a persistent source across the interval, while periodic cooling and local batch inference would remain plausible.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F3","day":14}}

{"thinking":"F3 showed a similar periodic line at the start, middle, and end of its elevated load. Check day 27, the first day after the load returned to baseline. A line at the same frequency would weaken its link to the extra load. If the line disappears, training, batch inference, and cooling equipment that cycled only under load remain plausible.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F3","day":27}}

{"thinking":"F3’s periodic line disappeared when its load returned to baseline. That ties the line to the extra load, which could come from training, batch inference, or cycling facility equipment. Staff answered the resale question but did not identify the equipment on F3. Obtain equipment IDs and circuit assignments so any GPU nodes can be checked with the verifier’s probe during day 26.","action":"staff","args":{"question":"Which equipment on F3 drew the extra roughly 11 MWh per day on days 2–26 and shut down before day 27? Please give the equipment IDs and circuit assignments so the load can be traced, and identify any F3 GPU node IDs available for probing at hour 610."}}

{"thinking":"F1 drew about 10 MWh more per day on days 18–28. That could reflect one large training run, several smaller runs, or batch inference. Sample Cluster A on day 24 to test whether GPU-to-GPU traffic is consistent with training. The tap alone cannot tell how many runs generated the traffic.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":24}}

{"thinking":"The escrow confirms that the scheduler records were submitted on time and match the current copies. Read the job entries to identify allocations, customer labels, and handoffs during the days 7–18 power plateau. Those details will guide independent checks of whether one run or several explain the measured traffic and power.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s peer traffic on day 26 was far above typical inference and consistent with low-communication training at the reported job size. Probe GPUs across the scheduled pool during that same day to test the batch inference label. The readings classify only the GPUs Borealis presents and cannot establish run membership.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0501","A-0700","A-0900","A-1100","A-1200"],"hour":610}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A's day-24 traffic on listed links is consistent with batch inference. The sustained F1 load could also reflect several small training runs, an accounting gap, or one coordinated run split across labels or using unlisted links. Check batch inference with live chip probes, independent runs with customer and link checks, accounting gaps against grid and bank records, and possible coordination with cross-cluster traffic and power spectra. Start with escrow to identify the jobs recorded during the F1 rise on days 18–28 and the F2 rise on days 10–11.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The mixed probe readings suggest cluster A may have been running both training and inference on day 26. A single day of elevated peer traffic leaves open a brief training job, several smaller runs, and sustained coordinated training. Sample cluster A near the start of the elevated power window to see whether the training-like traffic was already present.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":18}}

{"thinking":"Escrow confirms the scheduler records stayed unchanged, but it does not show which jobs they record or whether the labels are accurate. Read the job entries to identify what Borealis recorded during the F1 and F2 load increases and select nodes for a live probe during the F1 plateau.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A carried training-like peer traffic on days 18 and 26, and three sampled GPUs read as training on day 26. A detectable power line midway through the elevated-load window would give us an independent signature to compare across days and test whether one training process persisted. Batch inference and cooling can also produce a line, so its timing and frequency matter.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":22}}

{"thinking":"Repeated requests for F3 equipment and resale details yielded no verifiable identifiers or probe readings. Test a separate lead using the verifier’s optical tap on cluster A during Kestrel’s declared batch job and the outbound traffic increase. Inference-level traffic would support the batch label. Training-level traffic would justify checking how many GPUs participated, for how long, and whether they belonged to one run.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":14}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A showed elevated GPU-to-GPU traffic on days 12 and 17 during the same sustained power increase. That favors low-communication training over typical batch inference, but the tap cannot distinguish one coordinated run from several shorter runs. Use the fixed balance checks to reconcile the 700-GPU allocation with the metered load and identify any discrepancies that need independent follow-up.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The first probe reached only three of the 700 batch nodes, all near the start of the listed range. Day-24 traffic supports batch inference on the listed links. Probe five nodes farther into the batch allocation on day 27 to see whether their current signatures agree with the first sample or point to a mixed workload.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0762","A-0850","A-0937","A-1024","A-1200"],"hour":634}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s day-14 traffic supports the inference label for Kestrel’s batch job. The F3 load and the location of 600 delivered GPUs remain unresolved. Check the listed A–B links on day 26, when F3 was still drawing extra power and the scheduler recorded no training. Training-level traffic would give us an independent lead on coordination across the listed clusters. The tap cannot see unlisted links.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":26}}

{"thinking":"Eight probes across the declared batch pool and day-24 traffic on listed links favor legitimate batch inference. Separate small training runs, unrecorded activity, and one coordinated run using unlisted links or chips outside the probe sample remain possible. Run the fixed balance checks to see whether the recorded jobs account for the F1 and F2 energy increases and whether either feed has an unexplained load.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The limited day 28 probe again found mixed readings, with A-0501 and A-0700 reading as training on both days 26 and 28. To test whether one training process persisted or several shorter runs shared the pool, check whether the weak F1 line seen on days 22 and 26 was already present on day 18, when the tap measured elevated peer traffic. A similar line would support continuity but would leave the run’s GPU count unresolved.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":18}}

{"thinking":"The 0.54 Hz line could come from training, periodic batch inference, or a cooling controller. Check the same feed on day 29, the first day after the load returned to baseline. A similar line would weaken the link to the recorded batch job. If the line disappears, that ties it more closely to the elevated load but leaves the workload type open.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":29}}

{"thinking":"Grid meters show a simultaneous load increase on both GPU feeds on days 25–28. Batch inference, independent training jobs, and one coordinated run could all explain it. The sealed scheduler records can show which jobs and node allocations were recorded at the time and guide independent checks of workload type and coordination.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Two competing explanations remain plausible: the logged batch allocation was low-communication training, or it was inference alongside unrelated GPU traffic. Measure Cluster A on day 19, when F1 returned to baseline. If traffic also drops sharply, that ties the elevated traffic more closely to the allocation. If it persists, the earlier readings carry less weight as evidence about the batch job.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":19}}

{"thinking":"Grid meters show a simultaneous load increase on both clusters on days 25–28. Escrow confirms the scheduler records were preserved as filed. Read the recorded jobs, GPU allocations, and durations to identify which workloads to test independently for training and cross-cluster coordination.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The line appeared during the F1 load plateau and was absent after it ended. It could reflect training earlier in the plateau or a periodic batch or cooling load. Check F1 on day 27, when five chips in the declared batch pool read as inference, to see whether a similar line was present alongside those readings.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":27}}

{"thinking":"The similar F1 lines on days 18, 22, and 26 support continuity, but they cannot identify a run or count its GPUs. One sustained training run and a succession of smaller runs alongside batch inference both fit the measurements. Ask for the workload boundaries within bt-0480 and the expected traffic from each workload so those details can be tested against independent readings.","action":"staff","args":{"question":"What workloads ran under bt-0480 on days 18–28? For each, give its purpose, start and end hours, GPU ranges, and which GPUs exchanged data. What would account for the sustained GPU-to-GPU traffic and the training-like probe readings on days 26 and 28?"}}

{"thinking":"The cooling feed showed no line on day 22, when F1 showed a weak 1.13 Hz line. Sample cluster A’s peer traffic on that middle day to test whether training-like communication accompanied the F1 line between the elevated readings on days 18 and 26.
